clinicalPearls: A rare non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis presenting with recurrent crops of numerous symmetrical red-brown papules distributed widely over the trunk, face and proximal limbs.
It occurs predominantly in adults but is reported in children, and the eruption appears in successive waves.
Lesions are typically monomorphic, non-coalescing papules a few millimetres in diameter that spare or minimally involve mucous membranes.
By definition there is no visceral involvement, and the condition is regarded as a purely cutaneous, self-healing histiocytosis.
Individual papules tend to resolve spontaneously leaving transient macular hyperpigmentation, though new crops may recur over months to years.
Histology shows a monomorphous dermal infiltrate of histiocytes without significant lipidisation, foam cells or Touton giant cells, which are CD68 positive and CD1a and langerin negative.

It is widely considered an early or transitional form within the spectrum of cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses and may evolve towards xanthomatous forms such as juvenile xanthogranuloma or xanthoma disseminatum.
The diagnosis is partly one of exclusion, requiring differentiation from Langerhans cell histiocytosis and from histiocytoses with systemic involvement.
reference.pathophysiology: Generalised eruptive histiocytosis is a reactive proliferation of macrophage-derived dermal histiocytes belonging to the non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses. The lesional cells are non-lipidised histiocytes expressing macrophage markers such as CD68 while lacking the Langerhans cell markers CD1a and langerin and Birbeck granules. The characteristic absence of foam cells and Touton giant cells early in the disease, together with the tendency of some cases to acquire xanthomatous features over time, supports the concept that generalised eruptive histiocytosis represents an early, non-lipidised phase of the cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis spectrum that overlaps with benign cephalic histiocytosis, juvenile xanthogranuloma and xanthoma disseminatum. The self-healing crops reflect a self-limited reactive process with clearance of the histiocytic infiltrate rather than a persistent clonal neoplasm.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with histology and immunohistochemistry (CD68, factor XIIIa, CD1a, langerin)
Electron microscopy to confirm absence of Birbeck granules where required
Fasting serum lipid profile to exclude eruptive xanthoma
Clinical and laboratory review to exclude systemic histiocytosis and internal malignancy
Full blood count and inflammatory markers
Serum protein electrophoresis where an associated dyscrasia is suspected
Serial assessment to detect evolution towards a xanthomatous histiocytosis
redFlags: Hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy or cytopenias suggesting a systemic histiocytosis
Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss or night sweats
Bone pain or lytic lesions raising the possibility of Langerhans cell histiocytosis
Evolution of lesions with features suggesting an alternative malignant histiocytic disorder
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is favourable, with a chronic but ultimately self-healing course in which crops of papules regress spontaneously over months to years; a minority of cases evolve into other cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses, and treatment is generally unnecessary.
pitfalls: Making the diagnosis without adequately excluding Langerhans cell histiocytosis and systemic histiocytoses.
Mislabelling the eruption as eruptive xanthoma despite normal lipids and absent foam cells on histology.
Assuming permanence and over-treating a self-limiting condition.
Failing to follow patients for possible evolution towards xanthomatous forms.
Confusing recurrent crops with treatment failure.
references: WHO Classification of Histiocytoses and revised histiocytosis classification (current)
management: Reassurance and observation, since the eruption is purely cutaneous and typically self-healing, so active treatment is often unnecessary
Exclude mimics and associations by confirming histology, checking a fasting lipid profile to exclude eruptive xanthoma, and screening for systemic histiocytosis and internal malignancy
Symptomatic or cosmetic treatment of troublesome crops with options such as phototherapy, topical or systemic retinoids or corticosteroids where warranted
Longitudinal monitoring for evolution into another cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis such as xanthoma disseminatum
Dermatology follow-up with repeat biopsy if lesional morphology changes or xanthomatous features emerge
